article.title: ‘Monster data centers’ being built in Scotland for US tech companies met with protests
article.author: Ana Vračar
article.content: Thousands of people took to the streets of Edinburgh on Saturday, November 14, to protest against the massive expansion of data centers in Scotland. “Developers want to build monster data centers across Scotland and sell them on to big US tech companies,” the Stop AI Data Centers Scotland coalition wrote in the protest announcement. “There are over 20 already proposed and more in the pipeline, which would demand twice as much electricity as Scotland’s peak usage. This has huge consequences for our energy bills, water, health, communities, climate and nature.” Dozens of organizations that joined the coalition and protest – including climate justice associations, anti-war groups, and trade unions – have demanded accountability from the Scottish government: a pause on expansion plans, proper impact studies, and public consultations. “Decisions on AI data centers should be led by the people, not by big tech profits,” they said. “The people of Scotland must have a say on how our public resources are used.” Data centers return nothing to host communities Environmental organizations are warning that Scotland is becoming an increasingly attractive location for data centers due to “cheap land and cool climate.” But the Scottish government’s continuous referencing of “green data centers” – a term yet to be fully defined – as a development pathway cannot be dismissed as additional encouragement. This goes hand in hand with promises of data centers bringing more jobs, despite calculations showing these would number in the hundreds at best. Read more: Meta wants to build a $50 billion data center in Louisiana As a result, workers in Scotland would effectively bear the brunt of the massive data centers through increased costs of living and environmental devastation. “They demand massive public infrastructure and resource support,” emphasized Claire Robertson of the Edinburgh Trade Union Council, “yet return virtually no secure, permanent, or unionized jobs for the local communities forced to host them.” Environmental and health concerns The scale of many proposed data centers is a particular concern for the public. Action to Protect Rural Scotland (APRS) warned that planned hyper-scale data centers are one hundred times bigger than existing data centers. “The 1000 MW site proposed in Chapelcross, Annan would require the energy equivalent of a quarter of the entire peak demand of Scotland,” APRS found. “It would take Whitelees Windfarm, the largest onshore wind farm in the UK, eight years to generate the energy to power this site for just one year.” Read more: A massive AI data center transforms rural Utah into a national flashpoint Adding to fears about the impact on public infrastructure and the cost of living, health groups joined the mobilizations, emphasizing that data centers represent health hazards as well. The People’s Health Movement (PHM) Scotland is among the networks joining the protest, insisting that the mushrooming of data centers brings risks for heart and respiratory health through air pollution, the risk of skin diseases “arising from contaminated water entering the water supply,” and hearing loss and tinnitus as a consequence of noise pollution. PHM Scotland also highlighted the possibility of “increased mental health problems arising from loss of green space, noise pollution and the additional localized heat burden created by large data centers.” Ties to the military-industrial complex In addition to fears about consequences for local communities, organizations endorsing the protest expressed concerns about the potential international impact of hyper-scale data centers. “The rise of AI and the growing power of the tech oligarchy are intimately tied to the military-industrial complex,” said Coll McCail of Stop the War Scotland. “The Pentagon, for example, has already adopted an ‘AI first’ approach to warfare, spending 9 billion USD on data centers.” Protesters called for a pause on existing development plans, proper impact studies, and public consultations. Source: Climate Camp Scotland/Facebook “Closer to home, Peter Thiel’s Palantir has embedded itself within the Ministry of Defense, and the UK government has contracted Raytheon to train 60,000 soldiers in military AI every year. Scotland’s proposed data centers may yet be put in service for such aims, without sufficient public debate or discussion.” People’s Health Dispatch is a monthly bulletin published by the People’s Health Movement and Peoples Dispatch .
